main_argument_chains.claim: KROL is conditionally preferred to KREP and HLLR in the source's low-density/lower-parameter CA and factor-score comparisons.
support_steps: Construct baseline CA and shared metrics.
Define KROL/HLLR through altered lane incentives while retaining safety gates.
Compare aligned CA curves and factor-score curves.
Repeat the low-condition boundary in the conclusion.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Use the source ranking only as a scenario-bounded simulation result; require safety, calibration, uncertainty, and enforcement evidence before policy adoption.

main_argument_chains.claim: The ITS section is an idealized parameter counterfactual, not a demonstrated intelligent traffic controller.
support_steps: Set random braking probability to zero and lane-change probability to one.
Report KREP's lower flow and similar safety in the stated density band.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Treat ITS comparisons as a sensitivity scenario until an implementable control policy, information architecture, and uncertainty analysis are supplied.

warnings.warning: S1 uses != instead of an explicit below-vd condition.
Lane-index direction must be reconciled carefully with the prose return-to-right description.
Average-speed index ranges and denominator are not fully reconciled.
Lane-use rate is not normalized by capacity.
No seed, horizon, replication, uncertainty, or external calibration is supplied.
KROL lacks a complete conflict-resolution specification.
Factor analysis lacks sample construction, standardization, and adequacy diagnostics.
F2 safety direction lacks an independent safety validation.
No composite uncertainty-aware policy selection follows the published scores.
ITS changes probabilities without a controller or communication mechanism.
The repeated Figure 12 makes the ITS score-plot provenance unclear.
Authors report insufficient empirical data and rough behavioral estimates.

visualization_dispositions.analytical_purpose: Three visually separated Summary paragraphs route from base simulation and alternative rules through orientation transfer to ITS limiting conditions.
Connects traffic regimes and six scenario factors to flow, safety, velocity, and lane-change outputs before policy comparison.
A time-space field encodes vehicle speeds as text values and illustrates the paper's loop-road congestion narrative.
Three aligned density-response plots show flow, lane-changing frequency, and average velocity for the baseline CA.
Three aligned lane-count response plots hold the metric bundle fixed while varying number of lanes.
Three aligned maximum-speed response plots support the reported saturation discussion.
Large-vehicle-fraction plots expose a nonmonotonic lane-change response.
Lane-change-probability plots compare flow, lane changes, and velocity over a stated input range.
Random-braking plots show response directions under the same three-output layout.
Three-rule flow-versus-density comparison isolates KROL, KREP, and HLLR under common axes.
Three-rule lane-change-frequency comparison distinguishes an intermediate behavioral mechanism.
Three-rule average-speed comparison completes the direct counterfactual metric bundle.
Lane-use comparison visualizes how the loop redistributes occupancy between lanes.
Eigenvalue, proportion, and cumulative-proportion table supports the retained four-factor claim.
First rotated-loadings table relates X1-X5 to the four reported common factors.
Remaining rotated-loadings table completes X6-X8 for factor interpretation.
Standardized scoring-coefficient table provides the numerical inputs to F1-F4.
Factor-score comparison over density displays flow and safety score curves for all three rules.
Maximum-speed factor-score comparison shows scenario-dependent score responses.
Large-vehicle-fraction factor-score comparison carries the factor layer into a second sensitivity axis.
Lane-change-probability factor-score comparison tests rule ordering under a behavior parameter.
Random-braking factor-score comparison leads into the source's overall ranking statement.
ITS density-flow comparison uses altered RBP and LCP inputs to show an idealized counterfactual.
ITS lane-change-frequency comparison reports the intermediate behavior under the same scenario.
ITS average-speed comparison completes the ITS response set.
The paper reuses the factor-score visual after ITS simulation, leaving its new-data provenance to be checked.
